recommendationCandidates.title: Scope-aware privacy reset
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate a reset control that separately names local data, site sessions, open tabs, permissions, downloads and any actual network-path change.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can users predict what changes and what persists, and do controlled-origin storage tests match the displayed scope?
limitations: Baseline Chrome behavior must be checked first.
Avoid accidental data loss and terminology implying IP rotation or anonymity when neither occurs.

recommendationCandidates.title: Generic operating-system window titles
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate an opt-in setting to suppress page-derived OS window names while retaining usable window identification and assistive-technology behavior.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Does the mode suppress the intended title channel without breaking screen readers, task switchers and multi-window workflows?
limitations: No present Chrome gap is established.
This is one local disclosure control, not protection against all local observation.

recommendationCandidates.title: Coherent fingerprint-resistance preset
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate a defined, internally consistent preset rather than independent cosmetic spoofing toggles.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Across a representative population, does the preset reduce distinguishability while avoiding inconsistent signals and unacceptable site or accessibility breakage?
limitations: Requires population-based measurement and a threat model; no anonymity claim follows from a settings list.
Locale, media, graphics, accessibility and small-population uniqueness are material trade-offs.

recommendationCandidates.title: Background-service transparency and controls
recommendationCandidates.description: Expose purpose, recipient and trigger for optional browser-initiated connections, with understandable controls distinct from update and security-check delivery.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can a controlled network trace verify the described optional requests and their controls without silently disabling essential update or threat-protection flows?
limitations: Existing Chrome disclosures and controls require baseline verification.
Removing a service is not automatically a security improvement; update and malicious-download protection requirements remain explicit.

recommendationCandidates.title: Consent automation with truthful outcome reporting
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate cookie-consent automation that distinguishes rejection, partial configuration, cosmetic hiding and unhandled cases.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Across consent-manager fixtures, do the consent state and site behavior agree with the reported outcome, including iframe and regional variants?
limitations: A hidden banner is not evidence of rejected consent.
Baseline checks, explicit user intent, site overrides and changing consent-manager behavior require evaluation.

recommendationCandidates.title: Clear storage-lifetime boundaries and private tabs
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate mixed regular/private tab workflows with visible shared-state boundaries, deletion triggers and named persistent exceptions.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can users identify which tabs share ephemeral state, and do controlled login/storage tests confirm isolation and last-tab-close deletion?
limitations: Mixed UI can mislead users about session boundaries.
Private storage controls are not a network anonymity guarantee and must not be presented as one.

recommendationCandidates.title: Transparent URL and search interpretation
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate full-destination visibility, inspectable cleaned-link copying, suggestion-endpoint control and an explicit opt-out from automatic search interpretation.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can users inspect the original destination and copy a cleaned alternative without silent loss of functional parameters or unintended searches?
limitations: Signed URLs, authentication links, intranet addresses and meaningful query parameters need fixtures.
A manual clean-link action and automatic navigation-time protection are different capabilities.

recommendationCandidates.title: Accountless device-paired encrypted sync
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate user-held-key pairing and recovery without requiring a vendor identity account.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can devices pair, recover, revoke and delete supported sync data with understandable key-loss and already-local-copy behavior?
limitations: Requires cryptographic and metadata analysis, not inference from another vendor's policy.
Device compromise, recovery-code loss and data-type scope are separate concerns.

recommendationCandidates.title: One supported optional-AI control
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate a single supported control for enumerated browser AI entry points, proactive surfaces and related background requests.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Does disabling the control consistently affect the declared surfaces and traffic on each supported platform?
limitations: Chrome's existing controls and rollouts must be checked before identifying a gap.
The scope cannot promise removal of arbitrary AI-generated website content.

recommendationCandidates.title: Tree tabs and a feed side panel
recommendationCandidates.description: Evaluate research workflows using hierarchical tabs, subtree actions and searchable feed/unread controls with export and recovery.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Do these controls reduce task time in representative research sessions while remaining keyboard-accessible and usable at large tree/feed sizes?
limitations: Added interface complexity and accessible hierarchy need measurement.
Existing Chrome and extension workflows must be checked; no missing native feature is asserted here.

recommendationCandidates.title: Stable customization and extension contracts
recommendationCandidates.description: Investigate legitimate browser-UI customization and long-lived workflow needs behind classic extension systems, then evaluate supported APIs that retain contemporary permission and process boundaries.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Which concrete tasks need deeper UI affordances, and can stable APIs satisfy them without granting unbounded browser or native-plugin access?
limitations: Legacy XUL/NPAPI power is not a drop-in modern security design.
Measured demand and a compatibility corpus should precede any legacy protocol/plugin proposal.

recommendationCandidates.title: Public protection and lifecycle matrix
recommendationCandidates.description: Publish or improve a versioned matrix of platform/package-specific protections, exceptions, engine versions and automatic-update behavior, with source evidence and review dates.
recommendationCandidates.acceptanceQuestion: Can a user determine which controls are actually shipped for an OS/channel/package, which exceptions apply, and how updates are delivered?
limitations: Documentation can drift; each matrix row needs release/configuration evidence and an explicit review date.
A project's active label alone does not establish every package's update support or security coverage.

browsers.name: Tor Browser
browsers.engine: Firefox ESR-derived Gecko on desktop and GeckoView on Android; the 16.0.1 changelog names 153.7.0esr.
browsers.summary: A browser modified for Tor-network routing, site-keyed circuits, state isolation, and fingerprint resistance. Its network-anonymity design is distinct from ordinary private browsing or tracker blocking.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The inspected blog index and release bodies show 16.0.1 with Firefox security updates and Android-only 16.0.2 fixing a zlib-related breakage.

observedReleases.observation: Newest desktop-targeting announcement located in the inspected index.
Explicitly Android-only; the preceding 16.0.1 announcement names GeckoView 153.7.0esr.

platformBoundaries: 16.0 adds stable Linux AArch64 support and ends Linux x86 32-bit support.
The desktop offline manual and OS window-title option are not automatically Android features.
Only Tor Browser traffic is automatically routed through Tor; other applications are outside that scope.

quotations.text: This is an Android-only release
Updated Firefox to 153.7.0esr

limitations: Announcement dates remain unknown because cleaned bodies did not establish them.
Minimum OS versions and every distribution channel were not checked.
Logging into an identifying account still identifies that account; Tor does not erase information deliberately supplied to a site.
No anonymity-set size, privacy effectiveness, runtime behavior, or relative security result was measured.

browsers.name: Mullvad Browser
browsers.engine: Firefox ESR-derived browser developed with the Tor Project, without Tor-network patches; the 16.0 announcement names ESR 153. Exact engine patch level of 16.0.2 was not checked.
browsers.summary: A fingerprint-resistance and private-session browser usable with or without a VPN. It omits the Tor network, and clearing its session does not change the user's IP address.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The official latest-release API returned non-prerelease 16.0.2, updating uBlock Origin and the Mullvad extension and fixing DNS UI/error handling.
limitations: No mobile release was established.
The older hard-facts page is superseded on default DNS and reset-button terminology by the 16.0 announcement.
Documented build options disable EME/DRM and phishing/malware-protection functionality; restrictive fingerprint settings can affect sites.
These choices do not establish a net security ranking or Tor-equivalent anonymity.

browsers.name: LibreWolf
browsers.engine: Custom Firefox-derived browser; Gecko-family classification follows documented lineage rather than runtime inspection. The project says it follows Firefox stable.
platforms: Linux (distribution packages and x86_64 AppImage documented)
browsers.summary: A community Firefox derivative with privacy-oriented defaults and patches. Official installation pages supply current-looking download evidence, but release chronology and latest overall release could not be verified.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The three inspected installation pages offered 160.0-1. The official release endpoints were inaccessible, so active-release cadence, exact date, and latest overall version remain unknown.

observedReleases.edition: Inspected Windows, macOS and Linux download pages
observedReleases.observation: Download-link version only; not a verified latest release.

limitations: The homepage update statement is a vendor policy, not measured timely delivery to every package channel.
The source/releases and bsys6/releases endpoints returned HTTP 403; a newer version appearing only in search results was not accepted.
Windows scheduled updating has optional setup paths; Linux packaging has documented sandbox/process-isolation differences.
Safe Browsing, DRM and the built-in password manager are documented as disabled; no net-security conclusion follows.
No Tor-network anonymity or runtime privacy effectiveness was established.

browsers.name: ungoogled-chromium
browsers.engine: Chromium-derived common patches and configuration; Blink-family lineage. Platform-specific repositories supply additional build and packaging configuration.
browsers.summary: A narrow Chromium de-integration project prioritizing removal of Google web-service dependencies while retaining the Chromium experience. Most additional privacy/control tweaks require manual activation.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The official common-repository API returned non-prerelease 158.0.8127.36-1 with a publication timestamp, but an empty change body and no attached binary assets.
limitations: Latest source release is not proof of available, current, signed, or reproducible binaries for every platform.
Per-platform updater behavior and current Android support were not established.
The README documents Safe Browsing removal, impaired captive-portal detection, and a Windows change that does not set downloaded files' Zone Identifier.
Contributor binaries are not necessarily reproducible; the project qualifies their authenticity rather than guaranteeing it.
Service removal is not Tor anonymity or a measured security/privacy superiority claim.

browsers.name: Waterfox
browsers.engine: Desktop uses Gecko with a stated Firefox ESR maintenance model; its exact built engine version is unknown. The separate Android release body explicitly names Gecko 160.0, up from 159.0.
browsers.summary: A Gecko-based browser combining privacy-oriented defaults with private tabs, tree tabs, persistent status information, and feed workflows. Desktop and Android release lines are distinct.
platformBoundaries: Desktop download requirements include SSE4.2 for Windows/Linux and glibc 2.17 for Linux.
Firefox WebExtensions are documented as supported; Chrome-only extensions do not automatically transfer.
Current Waterfox must not be conflated with Waterfox Classic; Classic's lifecycle was not investigated.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: Official release APIs provide substantive desktop 6.7.8 and Android 1.2.11-2026445488 changes with separate publication timestamps.
limitations: The release page's Gecko 115.45 ESR advisory grouping is not reliable evidence of the desktop binary's engine version.
Desktop feature parity on Android is not established unless specifically cited.
OHTTP DNS separates documented relay/resolver knowledge; it does not establish anonymous browsing or a non-collusion guarantee.
No telemetry, memory, speed, privacy, or update-integrity measurement was performed.

browsers.name: Pale Moon
browsers.engine: Independently maintained Goanna rendering engine and Unified XUL Platform (UXP); not current Firefox or Chromium.
platforms: Other community-supported systems (FreeBSD build options are discussed)

No complete platform/update-channel inventory, patch-latency comparison, or modern-site test corpus was performed.

browsers.name: Basilisk
browsers.engine: Goanna / Unified XUL Platform (UXP), an independent pre-Servo Mozilla lineage. UXP originated from Firefox 52; Basilisk explicitly does not track current Firefox releases.
platforms: macOS (Intel, Apple Silicon and PowerPC builds listed)
browsers.summary: A classic-interface desktop browser focused on customization and long-lived workflows, with independently maintained compatibility changes and classic extension/plugin support.
platformBoundaries: Windows automatic updates are documented as supported; macOS downloads explicitly require manual updates; the FreeBSD archive also has no automatic updates.
The release introduces Intel 32-bit macOS builds and enables MIPS64EL Linux automatic updates.
Supporting an old OS means the app is offered there, not that the OS receives vendor security fixes.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The release body says Published 2026-11-01, the download page labels 2026.11.01 current, and the notes identify UXP commit 6b18be917d with security and compatibility changes.
limitations: No telemetry policy or Tor-like anonymity was established; neither is inferred from engine independence.
Compatibility is selective: :has() is disabled by default and the listed Intl.ListFormat polyfill is en-US-only.
Platform downloads and release notes were read, but execution, plugin behavior and update mechanisms were not tested.

browsers.name: DuckDuckGo Browser
browsers.engine: Windows: WebView2/Blink in a historical first-party architecture article. macOS/iOS: WebKit per platform documentation, with a WKWebView-linked macOS design. Android: Android WebView, with Chromium implementation provenance. Current engine-runtime versions were not inspected.
browsers.summary: Four platform applications using platform rendering components with a common privacy/product layer. Feature coverage, distribution constraints, and underlying engine behavior vary by platform.
platformBoundaries: The Windows help page says x86 updates end after version 0.170.0; it supplies no calendar cutoff.
The Mac App Store edition lacks the documented Bitwarden integration and local-file access of direct distribution.
The protection tables include platform-specific limitations and roadmap entries; uniform feature parity is not established.
browsers.maintenanceEvidence: The Q3 2026 update body documents ongoing product work, including Android Fire Tabs and AI-disable controls. Public Apple and Android repository documentation was also read.
limitations: Exact latest app builds and engine versions remain unknown. Historical launch articles do not establish continued beta status or current extension availability.
A guessed Windows repository URL returned 404; this does not establish Windows source availability or licensing.
The Apple README identifies a proprietary font dependency, so not every distributed asset can be called open source.
The policy documents a bat.bing.com conversion exception after DuckDuckGo ad clicks, not a blanket Microsoft-tracker exemption.
Tracker blocking, private sessions and encryption do not establish Tor-equivalent anonymity; no runtime effectiveness or comparative data-use result was measured.

features.title: Integrated Tor-network routing
features.description: Tor Browser is modified for use with Tor and routes its browser traffic through the Tor network. This network-identity property is distinct from merely deleting local history or blocking trackers.

quotations.text: heavily modified for use with the Tor network

limitations: Other applications are not automatically routed through Tor.
Identifying accounts or supplied personal information can identify the user to a site.
No anonymity effectiveness or traffic behavior was measured.

features.title: Site-keyed circuit isolation and circuit visualization
features.description: Different first-party sites use different Tor circuits even when they embed the same tracker. A desktop site-information control visualizes the current circuit; same-site tabs can share a circuit.
limitations: This is site-keyed isolation, not an independent identity for every tab.
The 16.0 announcement describes Android circuit display and a redesigned multi-path display as forthcoming; they are not counted as shipped here.
No routing or visualization test was performed.

features.title: Separate New Identity and New Tor Circuit controls
features.description: New Identity closes tabs/windows, clears private state and uses new circuits. New Tor Circuit for this Site instead reloads the site through another circuit without clearing its private state or unlinking activity.
limitations: New Identity stops current activity and downloads.
Changing circuits is a connection-recovery operation, not a substitute for identity reset.
Equivalent Android UI and actual clearing behavior were not established by a local test.

features.title: Fingerprint normalization and desktop letterboxing
features.description: The documentation describes reducing distinguishable fingerprint buckets through normalized attributes, font restrictions, user-agent normalization and window-size letterboxing on desktop.

quotations.text: it is practically impossible to make all Tor Browser users identical

limitations: The goal is reduced distinguishability, not perfect hiding of OS or device attributes.
Cross-platform behavior and fingerprint population effects were not measured.
Independent customization can alter the coherence of a fingerprint-resistance configuration.

This addresses window titles, not every form of local observation or device compromise.
No accessibility or OS-level behavior was tested.

Tracker-blocking coverage and site breakage were not measured.

features.title: RFP, normalized language and disabled WebGL
features.description: The project documents RFP, reporting en-US to websites, and disabling WebGL as parts of its fingerprint-resistance configuration.

quotations.text: Always display user language as
Disable WebGL

limitations: Language and graphics restrictions can affect localization and web applications.
The project's best-in-class wording is not adopted as a comparative finding.
No fingerprint or compatibility test was performed.

features.title: Ephemeral site data and reduced persistent caching
features.description: Documented defaults delete cookies and website data on close, disable disk cache and clear temporary files, reducing persistent local browsing state.

quotations.text: Delete cookies and website data on close.

limitations: Closing a session can end website logins.
Local deletion does not establish network anonymity or deletion of information already held by a site.
No storage-level erasure verification was performed.

features.title: Tracking-parameter removal and reduced speculative networking
features.description: The feature list describes stripping tracking elements from URLs, trimming cross-origin referrers, and disabling link prefetching and speculative connections.

quotations.text: Strip tracking elements from URLs, both natively and through uBO.
Disable link prefetching and speculative connections.

limitations: Parameter removal can interact with functional URLs; disabling speculation can affect loading behavior.
Neither effects nor compatibility were measured, and no Chrome default comparison is implied.

features.title: Quiet telemetry, suggestion and sponsored-content defaults
features.description: LibreWolf documents disabling telemetry, crash reporting, studies, search suggestions, recommendations, and distracting or sponsored home-page content.
limitations: No data collection is a project policy claim, not an independently verified zero-egress result.
No current binary defaults or service traffic were inspected.

features.title: Dedicated UI for privacy and security choices
features.description: A LibreWolf-specific UI exposes important privacy/security settings. The feature list separately describes an optional extension firewall and user-enabled Firefox Sync.
limitations: The extension firewall is documented as manually enabled and Sync disabled unless explicitly enabled; they are not unqualified default protections.
UI discoverability and effectiveness were not evaluated.

features.title: Removal of Google-service-specific functionality
features.description: The common project's primary objective is removal of dependency on Google web services, including disabling service-specific functionality, while remaining close to Chromium's user experience.
limitations: This describes an objective and patch design, not a verified absence of every browser network request.
Safe Browsing is among removed functions, so service removal cannot be treated as a blanket security improvement.
Binary behavior and package-specific differences were not tested.

features.title: Fail-safe blocking of substituted internal domains
features.description: The README describes replacing certain internal Google domains with non-existent qjz9zk alternatives and blocking the browser's own requests to those alternatives at runtime.
limitations: The mechanism targets substituted internal requests, not arbitrary third-party web content.
The patch implementation and runtime network behavior were not audited.

features.title: Source binary pruning
features.description: The common build approach removes pre-made binaries from source and uses user-provided alternatives where possible, as described in the repository's objectives and feature list.
platforms: Shared source/build workflow; platform packaging varies
limitations: Source pruning is not proof that a contributor binary is reproducible or authentic.
No build was performed; the common release itself contained no binary assets.

features.title: Explicit address-bar search and suggestion controls
features.description: The README documents a No Search omnibox provider to disable searching and a Suggestions URL field in the search-engine editor for custom suggestion endpoints.
limitations: Availability and defaults can vary by build and version.
No address-versus-search behavior, suggestion network request, or BSD package was tested.

features.title: Additional configuration flags and transparent URL display
features.description: The project documents new command-line switches and flags, along with disabling automatic omnibox URL formatting such as protocol stripping and hidden parameters.
limitations: The README says many added features require manual activation; this record does not assert every option is enabled by default.
Flags are not necessarily stable, supported user-facing contracts.
Specific builds and URL-rendering behavior were not exercised.

features.title: Popup-to-tab behavior
features.description: The common feature overview documents forcing pop-up windows into tabs as a browser-control choice.
limitations: Default activation and exact behavior in particular packages were not established.
Compatibility with authentication pop-ups and application-style windows needs testing.

features.title: Private tabs alongside regular tabs
features.description: Desktop private tabs sit alongside regular tabs, share a separate private container, and clear that container's site data when the last private tab closes while the normal session continues.
limitations: Private tabs share that container with one another; this is not per-tab identity isolation.
Private-tab storage is not network anonymity.
Erasure, UI clarity and Android parity were not tested.

features.title: DNS over Oblivious HTTP
features.description: The product page describes encrypting DNS queries and sending them through an OHTTP relay, separating the relay's view of the connecting client from the resolver's view of the query.
limitations: Relay/resolver separation is a documented mechanism, not a verified non-collusion or retention guarantee.
DNS privacy is not anonymous browsing; site traffic and identifying accounts remain separate concerns.
Fallback behavior, traffic flow and Android support were not tested.

features.title: Tree-structured tabs and subtree actions
features.description: The product page describes nesting pages under their opener, collapsing branches and moving entire subtrees to organize related browsing tasks.
limitations: Keyboard access, assistive-technology behavior and large-tree scaling were not evaluated.
Android parity and productivity gains were not established.

features.title: Persistent status-bar URL display
features.description: A desktop status bar exposes the full destination when hovering over links, alongside loading progress and keyboard-shortcut information, rather than using a transient overlay.
limitations: Screen-space, accessibility and destination-disclosure usability were not evaluated.
This is a desktop description, not established mobile behavior or a Chrome gap.

features.title: Feeds sidebar with search, unread counts and recovery
features.description: Desktop 6.7.8 adds a feed sidebar with search and unread counts, a refresh-all action, and feed-subscription backup/recovery and import/export fixes.
limitations: Active bug fixing and recovery features do not establish complete feed-format compatibility.
No subscription, recovery or usability workflow was tested.

features.title: Built-in ad blocking and documented telemetry removal
features.description: The product page describes built-in ad blocking, removal of browser telemetry and a no-data-collection policy as parts of its default product design.
limitations: Collection and efficacy statements are vendor claims, not a network audit.
6.7.8 fixes external links failing with the content blocker, demonstrating a documented compatibility interaction.
Android parity and net privacy or performance effects were not established.

features.title: Optional Android sensitive-screen overlay protection
features.description: The separate Android release adds Protect sensitive screens on Android 12+, hiding other apps' floating windows while password, payment-card or saved-address editing screens are displayed.
features.defaultState: Off by default according to the Android release body.
limitations: This is an Android-only documented control for named sensitive screens, not a general guarantee against local observation or compromise.
No overlay or device test was performed.

features.title: Experimental iCloud Passwords integration
features.description: Desktop 6.7.8 documents experimental integration with Apple's password software for filling passwords and verification codes; enabling it also selects iCloud for new password saves.
limitations: Requires Apple's password software and explicit enablement.
Experimental support is not guaranteed parity with every password-manager integration.
No credential data was accessed and no integration was exercised.

features.title: Deep XUL extension customization
features.description: Pale Moon documents XUL extensions capable of changing browser functions and interface behavior beyond web-content-only customization.
limitations: This is a different extension ecosystem from current Chrome/Firefox WebExtensions.
Extension power is not itself evidence of a desirable security boundary or a verified Chrome API gap.
No extension was installed or audited.

features.title: Legacy NPAPI plugin support
features.description: The homepage documents support for legacy native plugins through NPAPI; release notes discuss packaging choices for plugin dependencies.
limitations: Plugin availability depends on OS, architecture, build and plugin dependencies.
Browser support does not mean an old plugin is maintained or safe.
No plugin runtime testing or proposal to restore NPAPI in Chrome is implied.

features.title: Native RSS and Atom feed support
features.description: The product page lists native RSS/Atom feed support as part of retained browser content handling.
limitations: Feed parsing, subscriptions and reader usability were not exercised.
No feed feature comparison with Chrome was performed.

features.title: Retained FTP and XSLT functionality
features.description: The homepage lists native FTP and XML transformations through XSLT among supported browser capabilities.
limitations: Retention may serve long-lived workflows but is not a blanket recommendation to restore legacy implementations in Chrome.
The publisher's claims about Chrome removal schedules were not used as Chrome baseline evidence.
No protocol, parser or compatibility test was performed.

features.title: Deliberately minimal telemetry and product integrations
features.description: The project states that the browser contains no ads, telemetry, data gathering, DRM or AI integration, describing a deliberate product and service policy.
limitations: This is a vendor policy/design statement, not a verified zero-egress claim.
No runtime audit, privacy-effectiveness measure or net-security comparison was performed.

features.title: Built-in compatibility shims and overrides
features.description: 35.0.0 adds default compatibility shims/polyfills for selected APIs and documents adjustable compatibility behavior, including form parsing and user-agent compatibility settings.
limitations: The notes warn that strict content security policies can interfere and shims do not work universally.
35.0.2 disables :has() by default for performance, illustrating a compatibility trade-off.
No modern-site corpus or performance benchmark was run.

features.title: Traditional customizable desktop interface
features.description: Basilisk documents a traditional desktop interface with extensive customization and an emphasis on stable, long-lived workflows rather than following current Firefox interface changes.
limitations: Predictability and long-term usability are design goals, not measured user outcomes.
No UI or accessibility testing was performed.

features.title: Classic XUL and overlay-based extensions
features.description: The project explicitly preserves classic XUL and overlay-based extension capabilities on its independently maintained UXP platform.
limitations: Chrome Web Store or current Firefox extension compatibility is not implied.
The power or longevity of an extension system does not establish its security properties.
No extension was installed or audited.

features.title: NPAPI plugin support
features.description: Basilisk documents retained native plugin support through NPAPI as part of its classic desktop compatibility surface.
limitations: An individual plugin must match its platform and architecture; compatible plugins were not inventoried.
Legacy support is distinct from plugin maintenance or safety and is not a blanket Chrome recommendation.

features.title: Integrated compatibility polyfills and explicit switches
features.description: The 2026.11.01 notes list Intl, Streams and other polyfills, a Microsoft-specific WebAuthn shim, and preferences for CSS :has() and strict form-element parsing.
limitations: The listed Intl.ListFormat polyfill is en-US-only and :has() is off by default because of documented performance problems.
A shim or compatibility preference does not establish complete API conformance.
No compatibility or performance experiment was run.

features.title: Tracker-request blocking with public lists and local surrogates
features.description: DuckDuckGo describes identifying tracker requests with public lists and preventing their loading. Local surrogate scripts can replicate expected APIs without the tracking calls to reduce tracker-dependent breakage.
limitations: Most is a vendor coverage claim, not a measured result here.
The documentation includes temporary compatibility exceptions and separate treatment of infrastructure domains.
The bat.bing.com conversion exception applies after DuckDuckGo ad clicks; it is not a blanket Microsoft-tracker exemption.
The described protection does not establish Tor anonymity or native Chrome absence.

features.title: Automatic cookie-consent handling with limited coverage
features.description: The documentation describes attempting to minimize consented cookies and close a detected pop-up. Where preference management is unavailable it may only hide the pop-up using filter or cosmetic rules.
features.defaultState: Documented as enabled by default on supported app platforms.
limitations: Cosmetic hiding is not proof that consent was rejected or cookies were prevented.
Android iframe script-injection limits prevent handling some sites; coverage is incomplete and changes over time.
Support for the DuckDuckGo extension is distinct from the host Chrome browser's native capabilities.
No consent-manager corpus or consent-state test was performed.

features.title: Fire Button, Fireproof exceptions and isolated Fire sessions
features.description: The Fire Button exposes scoped deletion of browsing data. Fireproof sites retain selected state, while Fire Windows on desktop and Fire Tabs on mobile isolate activity from regular sessions and delete their session data on closing.
limitations: The Fire Button does not delete Fireproof first-party state, bookmarks, downloaded files or some app/search settings.
The isolated-session and erasure statements are documented semantics, not forensic guarantees verified here.
These local/session controls do not change the network-identity model or establish anonymity.

features.title: Accountless end-to-end encrypted Sync & Backup
features.description: The policy describes syncing supported data with encryption on devices and decryption keys held on connected devices. Pairing uses recovery/QR codes without requiring a personal identity account.
limitations: The architecture and access promises were not independently cryptographically audited.
Recovery-code custody and device access matter; supported data types and optional restore behavior need platform-specific verification.
The policy says data not accessed for 18 months is deleted from servers; deleting server data does not remove already-local copies.
Accountless synchronization is not Tor anonymity.

features.title: Consolidated optional-AI opt-out
features.description: Q3 2026 updates document a Use DuckDuckGo Without AI control that disables Duck.ai, hides AI-assisted search answers and applies a filter for known AI spam sites in image search results.
limitations: The scope is the vendor's enumerated browser/service surfaces, not removal of arbitrary AI-generated web content.
The exact first app version and all network effects were not established.
No Chrome absence or comparable-control default is asserted.

features.title: Layered tracking controls with platform-specific coverage
features.description: The protection matrix separately documents CNAME handling, fingerprint API changes, link/referrer controls, cookie restrictions, HTTPS upgrading and Global Privacy Control. These are different mechanisms with different platform coverage, not a single uniform guarantee.

platformCoverage.documentedScope: Windows/Android list-based handling; macOS/iOS coverage is a subset with a stated roadmap for usability limitations.
The Android table excludes iframe overrides because of WebView script-injection limitations.

Platform tables distinguish implemented expiry from Windows and Android roadmap items; the generic introduction is not proof of uniform coverage.

A manual Copy Clean Link control is distinct from automatic link protection and does not establish parity with the automatic-navigation table.
Chrome extension limitations and historical Topics comparisons do not establish native Chrome gaps or current lifecycle facts.
No tracking effectiveness, GPC compliance, HTTPS coverage or cookie-expiry test was run.

submission.reason: Research finding only; any publication or upstream submission is owned by the coordinating session.

limitations: This lane records primary-source documentation and release metadata, not hands-on browser results. No local reproduction, install, network capture, source-code audit, performance benchmark or fingerprint-population experiment was performed.
Chrome absence, parity, defaults, rollout and platform coverage remain not established for every candidate; the dedicated baseline lane must determine them.

Tor-network anonymity, ordinary tracker resistance, local data retention, DNS privacy, security and compatibility are distinct properties. No blanket browser ranking or unmeasured superiority is claimed.

Latest observed records are retrieval snapshots, not guarantees that every distribution channel is current. LibreWolf's latest overall release and date, DuckDuckGo's latest app versions, and several exact engine patch levels remain unknown.
LibreWolf release endpoints returned HTTP 403, as did the raw Tor build changelog; public installation pages and release-announcement bodies supplied the narrower evidence retained here.
A guessed DuckDuckGo Windows repository returned HTTP 404 and a guessed sync-help path returned generic text; neither failure establishes absence. The actual Sync & Backup policy was read instead.
Sources are mutable. The older Mullvad hard-facts DNS/reset descriptions conflict with the newer 16.0 announcement; release-specific evidence is used for those fields.
Unverified extraction dates were discarded rather than converted into publication facts. Quarterly update periods and release dates are explicitly distinguished from unknown page publication dates.

Vendor claims about zero telemetry, no collection, nearly identical fingerprints, stronger protection or relative resource usage were not independently audited. Documentation is evidence of the claim or mechanism, not proof of effectiveness.

Recommendation candidates are unsubmitted hypotheses with proposed acceptance questions. The single issue is a source inconsistency, not a reproduced browser defect or an upstream report submitted by this project.

The 48 feature records preserve all 46 substantive feature-table rows from the completed research and separately retain two documented Waterfox capabilities from its release discussion. No additional research or cross-lane build work was performed.
